          -s EvolKV at every budget, both searching once ($+1.3$ to $+2.1
          -$) and per budget at EvolKV's compute ($+0.8$ to $+1.7$, Appen
          -dix~\ref{app:cost}), and even searched once, MOSAIC's winner o
          -utperforms EvolKV's per-budget searches at every budget where 
          -both ran (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv}).                          
      127 +\textbf{MOSAIC versus EvolKV.}\label{sec:intro-evolkv} The clo
          +sest prior work, EvolKV \citep{yu2025evolkv}, searches per-lay
          +er budgets with CMA-ES \citep{hansen2001cmaes} group by group,
          + eight layers at a time, at a target budget fixed in advance. 
          +MOSAIC instead searches all layer budgets jointly, so one sear
          +ch spans about $10^{40}$ times more allocations than one EvolK
          +V group search, across a budget--score Pareto front, selects a
          + reusable anchor, and optionally refines it at each deployment
          + budget; on Code it beats EvolKV at every budget, both searchi
          +ng once ($+1.3$ to $+2.1$) and per budget at EvolKV's compute 
          +($+0.8$ to $+1.7$, Appendix~\ref{app:cost}), and even searched
          + once, MOSAIC's winner outperforms EvolKV's per-budget searche
          +s at every budget where both ran (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv}).  
      128  
      129  Our contributions are: (i) MOSAIC, a four-stage workflow (join
           t per-layer search, budget--score exploration, winner rescalin
           g, optional per-budget refinement) whose single search yields 
           a winner that transfers across budgets without further search;
            (ii) an evaluation across four eviction methods, two models a
           nd two benchmarks, where MOSAIC improves over uniform allocati
           on for every method, with gains of up to +48 points on RULER; 
           and (iii) an analysis of the learned allocations, which favour
            a small set of middle layers.
      130  
      131  \section{Related Work}
      132  
      133 -\textbf{Token eviction.} Eviction methods reduce KV-cache memo
          -ry by retaining only the tokens judged important. H2O \citep{z
          -hang2023h2o} keeps ``heavy hitters'', tokens with high accumul
          -ated attention, together with a window of recent tokens. SnapK
          -V \citep{li2024snapkv} selects, for each attention head, the p
          -rompt positions that receive the most attention from an observ
          -ation window at the end of the prompt. L2Norm \citep{devoto202
          -4l2norm} keeps the tokens whose keys have the lowest $L_2$ nor
          -m, which correlates with high attention, without computing att
          -ention scores. KeyDiff \citep{park2025keydiff} also avoids att
          -ention scores, keeping keys that are geometrically distinctive
          - from the others, which makes it compatible with FlashAttentio
          -n. QUOKA \citep{jones2026quoka} selects key-value pairs for pr
          -efill from the keys aligned with a subset of representative qu
          -eries. These methods decide which tokens to keep; how much cac
          -he each layer should receive is a separate question, which MOS
          -AIC addresses.                                                
      133 +\textbf{Token eviction.} Eviction methods reduce KV-cache memo
          +ry by retaining only the tokens judged important. H2O \citep{z
          +hang2023h2o} keeps ``heavy hitters'', tokens with high accumul
          +ated attention, together with a window of recent tokens; Strea
          +mingLLM \citep{xiao2024streamingllm} keeps the first tokens as
          + attention sinks plus a recent window, Scissorhands \citep{liu
          +2023scissorhands} keeps tokens whose importance persists acros
          +s decoding steps, and FastGen \citep{ge2024fastgen} chooses a 
          +compression policy per head by profiling. SnapKV \citep{li2024
          +snapkv} selects, for each attention head, the prompt positions
          + that receive the most attention from an observation window at
          + the end of the prompt. L2Norm \citep{devoto2024l2norm} keeps 
          +the tokens whose keys have the lowest $L_2$ norm, which correl
          +ates with high attention, without computing attention scores. 
          +KeyDiff \citep{park2025keydiff} also avoids attention scores, 
          +keeping keys that are geometrically distinctive from the other
          +s, which makes it compatible with FlashAttention \citep{dao202
          +4flashattention2}. QUOKA \citep{jones2026quoka} selects key-va
          +lue pairs for prefill from the keys aligned with a subset of r
          +epresentative queries. Quest \citep{tang2024quest} keeps the f
          +ull cache but loads only the pages relevant to each query, whi
          +le KV quantization \citep{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant} and c
          +ross-layer merging \citep{liu2024minicache} shrink the cache i
          +n other dimensions; all are complementary to eviction. These m
          +ethods decide which tokens to keep; how much cache each layer 
          +should receive is a separate question, which MOSAIC addresses.
      134  
      135 -\textbf{Static and dynamic budget allocation.} A second line o
          -f work allocates a fixed total budget non-uniformly instead of
          - changing how tokens are scored. Dynamic methods recompute the
          - allocation for every prompt, as dynamic quantization computes
          - its ranges at run time: Ada-KV \citep{feng2025adakv} allocate
          -s budget adaptively across the heads of a layer, and CAKE \cit
          -ep{qin2025cake} derives per-layer budgets from layer preferenc
          -es measured on each prompt's attention patterns. Static method
          -s fix the allocation before inference: PyramidKV \citep{cai202
          -5pyramidkv} assigns layer budgets following a hand-designed py
          -ramidal shape, larger in lower layers and smaller in higher on
          -es. MOSAIC is static in the sense of static quantization, cali
          -brating the allocation offline for each model and eviction met
          -hod. Closest to our work, EvolKV \citep{yu2025evolkv} treats p
          -er-layer budgets as optimization variables, partitions layers 
          -into groups, and runs evolutionary search on one group at a ti
          -me against downstream task score at one target budget; its mai
          -n results then extend that allocation to larger budgets by pro
          -portional rescaling, without further optimization. MOSAIC shar
          -es this rescaling step but finds the allocation to rescale dif
          -ferently, searching all layers jointly across budgets rather t
          -han at one target budget (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv}).          
      135 +\textbf{Static and dynamic budget allocation.} A second line o
          +f work allocates a fixed total budget non-uniformly instead of
          + changing how tokens are scored. Dynamic methods recompute the
          + allocation for every prompt, as dynamic quantization computes
          + its ranges at run time: Ada-KV \citep{feng2025adakv} allocate
          +s budget adaptively across the heads of a layer, CAKE \citep{q
          +in2025cake} derives per-layer budgets from layer preferences m
          +easured on each prompt's attention patterns, and SqueezeAttent
          +ion \citep{wang2025squeezeattention} splits layers into two gr
          +oups by how much attention changes their hidden states and shi
          +fts budget between them. Static methods fix the allocation bef
          +ore inference: PyramidKV \citep{cai2025pyramidkv} assigns laye
          +r budgets following a hand-designed pyramidal shape, larger in
          + lower layers and smaller in higher ones, and PyramidInfer \ci
          +tep{yang2024pyramidinfer} likewise keeps less context in deepe
          +r layers; HeadKV \citep{fu2025headkv} and DuoAttention \citep{
          +xiao2025duoattention} fix head-level allocations offline, from
          + head importance scores or a learned split into retrieval and 
          +streaming heads. MOSAIC is static in the sense of static quant
          +ization, calibrating the allocation offline for each model and
          + eviction method. Closest to our work, EvolKV \citep{yu2025evo
          +lkv} treats per-layer budgets as optimization variables, parti
          +tions layers into groups, and runs evolutionary search on one 
          +group at a time against downstream task score at one target bu
          +dget; its main results then extend that allocation to larger b
          +udgets by proportional rescaling, without further optimization
          +. MOSAIC shares this rescaling step but finds the allocation t
          +o rescale differently, searching all layers jointly across bud
          +gets rather than at one target budget (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv
          +}).                                                           
      136  
      137 -\textbf{Neural architecture search.} Multi-objective NAS trade
          -s off competing goals such as accuracy and latency along a Par
          -eto front \citep{elsken2018neural}. MOSAIC adopts this multi-o
          -bjective formulation for KV-cache allocation but uses its own 
          -search procedure (Section~\ref{sec:method}): a classifier-guid
          -ed optimizer built for this problem, which needs only a few hu
          -ndred evaluations per search.                                 
      137 +\textbf{Neural architecture search.} Multi-objective NAS trade
          +s off competing goals such as accuracy and latency along a Par
          +eto front \citep{elsken2018neural}; Once-for-All \citep{cai202
          +0ofa} trains one network and specializes it to many hardware b
          +udgets, much as MOSAIC searches once and rescales to many cach
          +e budgets. Gradient-based NAS \citep{liu2019darts} does not ap
          +ply here, as the task score is not differentiable in the per-l
          +ayer token budgets. MOSAIC adopts this multi-objective formula
          +tion for KV-cache allocation but uses its own search procedure
          + (Section~\ref{sec:method}): a classifier-guided optimizer bui
          +lt for this problem, which needs only a few hundred evaluation
          +s per search.

      140  \label{sec:method}
     ...
      146  
      147  \textbf{Search space.} Stage 1's grid of $|G|$ levels per laye
           r holds $|G|^L$ configurations ($5^{32} \approx 2.3\times10^{2
           2}$ or $7^{32} \approx 1.1\times10^{27}$ for $L = 32$) spannin
           g every average budget from 64 to the grid cap, and at a fixed
            budget $B$ the integer allocations in $[64, 4096]^L$ with mea
           n $B$ number about $10^{69}$ at B128 and $10^{105}$ at B1024. 
           One EvolKV search varies only eight layers with the other $L -
            8$ fixed: even ignoring its budget penalty, that is at most $
           4033^8 \approx 10^{29}$ allocations, about $10^{40}$ times few
           er than one MOSAIC search at B128 (Appendix~\ref{app:repro}). 
           A search evaluates at most 200 of them in Stage 1 and 150 in S
           tage 4 (Appendix~\ref{app:repro}), so every layer budget must 
           be chosen jointly from a vanishing fraction of the space.
      148  
      149 -\textbf{Search step.} All stages share one classifier-guided B
          -ayesian optimization procedure. After each evaluation, the arc
          -hive is non-dominated sorted, an MLP classifier (two hidden la
          -yers of 32 units) is trained to separate the rank-1 configurat
          -ions from the rest, and differential evolution maximizes the c
          -lassifier's probability of rank 1 over $[0,1]^L$ to propose th
          -e next configuration, one evaluation per iteration. We call th
          -ese BO proposals; stopping rules are in Appendix~\ref{app:repr
          -o}.                                                           
      149 +\textbf{Search step.} All stages share one classifier-guided B
          +ayesian optimization procedure \citep[cf.][]{tiao2021bore}. Af
          +ter each evaluation, the archive is non-dominated sorted \cite
          +p{deb2002nsga2}, an MLP classifier (two hidden layers of 32 un
          +its) is trained to separate the rank-1 configurations from the
          + rest, and differential evolution \citep{storn1997differential
          +} maximizes the classifier's probability of rank 1 over $[0,1]
          +^L$ to propose the next configuration, one evaluation per iter
          +ation. We call these BO proposals; stopping rules are in Appen
          +dix~\ref{app:repro}.

      162  \textbf{Tasks.}\label{sec:method-tasks} MOSAIC searches separa
           tely for each task and eviction method. LongBench has four Eng
           lish task categories, each a group of datasets: Single-Doc QA 
           (NarrativeQA, Qasper, MultiFieldQA-en), Multi-Doc QA (HotpotQA
           , 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue), Summarization (GovReport, QMSum, 
           MultiNews) and Code (LCC, RepoBench-P); a category's score is 
           the mean over its datasets. We search each LongBench category 
           separately because their tasks and metrics differ (F1 for QA, 
           ROUGE-L for summarization, edit similarity for code). RULER's 
           11 retrieval subtasks at 4K context share one metric (string-m
           atch accuracy), so a single search covers all of them. Stages 
           1--2 run once per (task, method) and Stages 3--4 once per targ
           et budget; we call each (task, method, budget) a \emph{cell}.
      163  
      164 -\textbf{Stage 1 (Unconstrained Multi-Budget NAS):} Search a di
          -screte per-layer grid of powers of two with no budget constrai
          -nt, from 64 up to 4096 on RULER and up to 1024 or 4096 on Long
          -Bench (Appendix~\ref{app:repro}). The initial design has 64 po
          -ints: the uniform allocation at every grid level plus Latin Hy
          -percube samples. Guided iterations then trace out the budget--
          -score Pareto front. Because this search must rank allocations 
          -across the whole budget range, and runs only once per (task, m
          -ethod), it uses a larger calibration subsample on LongBench (3
          -0\%; case study in Appendix~\ref{app:calib}); on RULER it uses
          - 10\%, which already ranks faithfully (Appendix~\ref{app:calib
          -}).

          -compression policy per head by profiling. SnapKV \citep{li2024
          -snapkv} selects, for each attention head, the prompt positions
          - that receive the most attention from an observation window at
          - the end of the prompt. L2Norm \citep{devoto2024l2norm} keeps

          -ates with high attention, without computing attention scores.

          -n other dimensions; all are complementary to eviction. These m
          -ethods decide which tokens to keep; how much cache each layer

      135 -\textbf{Static and dynamic budget allocation.} A second line o
          -f work allocates a fixed total budget non-uniformly instead of
          - changing how tokens are scored. Dynamic methods recompute the
          - allocation for every prompt, as dynamic quantization computes
          - its ranges at run time: Ada-KV \citep{feng2025adakv} allocate
          -s budget adaptively across the heads of a layer, CAKE \citep{q
          -in2025cake} derives per-layer budgets from layer preferences m
          -easured on each prompt's attention patterns, and SqueezeAttent
          -ion \citep{wang2025squeezeattention} splits layers into two gr
          -oups by how much attention changes their hidden states and shi
          -fts budget between them. Static methods fix the allocation bef
          -ore inference: PyramidKV \citep{cai2025pyramidkv} assigns laye
          -r budgets following a hand-designed pyramidal shape, larger in
          - lower layers and smaller in higher ones, and PyramidInfer \ci
          -tep{yang2024pyramidinfer} likewise keeps less context in deepe

          +ers and smaller in higher ones, as does PyramidInfer \citep{ya
          +ng2024pyramidinfer}; HeadKV \citep{fu2025headkv} and DuoAttent
          +ion \citep{xiao2025duoattention} fix head-level allocations of
          +fline. MOSAIC is static in the sense of static quantization, c

          +s per-layer budgets as optimization variables, partitions laye
          +rs into groups, and runs evolutionary search on one group at a
          + time against downstream task score at one target budget; its 
          +main results then extend that allocation to larger budgets by 
          +proportional rescaling, without further optimization. MOSAIC s
          +hares this rescaling step but finds the allocation to rescale 
          +differently, searching all layers jointly across budgets rathe
          +r than at one target budget (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv}).

          -s off competing goals such as accuracy and latency along a Par

          -0ofa} trains one network and specializes it to many hardware b
          -udgets, much as MOSAIC searches once and rescales to many cach
          -e budgets. Gradient-based NAS \citep{liu2019darts} does not ap
          -ply here, as the task score is not differentiable in the per-l

          -tion for KV-cache allocation but uses its own search procedure
          - (Section~\ref{sec:method}): a classifier-guided optimizer bui
          -lt for this problem, which needs only a few hundred evaluation
          -s per search.

      481 +\section{Further Related Work}                                
      482 +\label{app:related}                                           
      483 +                                                              
      484 +\textbf{Complementary cache compression.} Other techniques shr
          +ink the KV cache along axes that per-layer allocation leaves u
          +ntouched and can be combined with it: Quest \citep{tang2024que
          +st} keeps the full cache but loads only the pages relevant to 
          +each query, KIVI \citep{liu2024kivi} and KVQuant \citep{hooper
          +2024kvquant} quantize keys and values to a few bits, and MiniC
          +ache \citep{liu2024minicache} merges the caches of adjacent la
          +yers.                                                         
      485 +                                                              
      486 +\textbf{Searching once for many budgets.} Once-for-All \citep{
          +cai2020ofa} trains one network and specializes it to many hard
          +ware budgets; MOSAIC similarly searches once and rescales the 
          +result to many cache budgets. Gradient-based NAS such as DARTS
          + \citep{liu2019darts} does not apply here, because the task sc
          +ore is not differentiable in the per-layer token budgets.

      131  \section{Related Work}
      132  
      133 -\textbf{Token eviction.} Eviction methods reduce KV-cache memo
          -ry by retaining only the tokens judged important. H2O \citep{z
          -hang2023h2o} keeps ``heavy hitters'', tokens with high accumul
          -ated attention, together with a window of recent tokens; Strea
          -mingLLM \citep{xiao2024streamingllm} keeps attention-sink and 
          -recent tokens, Scissorhands \citep{liu2023scissorhands} tokens
          - whose importance persists, and FastGen \citep{ge2024fastgen} 
          -a per-head policy found by profiling. SnapKV \citep{li2024snap
          -kv} selects, for each attention head, the prompt positions tha
          -t receive the most attention from an observation window at the
          - end of the prompt. L2Norm \citep{devoto2024l2norm} keeps the 
          -tokens whose keys have the lowest $L_2$ norm, which correlates
          - with high attention, without computing attention scores. KeyD
          -iff \citep{park2025keydiff} also avoids attention scores, keep
          -ing keys that are geometrically distinctive from the others, w
          -hich makes it compatible with FlashAttention \citep{dao2024fla
          -shattention2}. QUOKA \citep{jones2026quoka} selects key-value 
          -pairs for prefill from the keys aligned with a subset of repre
          -sentative queries. These methods decide which tokens to keep; 
          -how much cache each layer should receive is a separate questio
          -n, which MOSAIC addresses.                                    
      133 +\textbf{Token eviction.} Eviction methods reduce KV-cache memo
          +ry by retaining only the tokens judged important. H2O \citep{z
          +hang2023h2o} keeps ``heavy hitters'', tokens with high accumul
          +ated attention, together with a window of recent tokens, as do
          + StreamingLLM \citep{xiao2024streamingllm}, Scissorhands \cite
          +p{liu2023scissorhands} and FastGen \citep{ge2024fastgen} with 
          +sink, persistent and per-head criteria. SnapKV \citep{li2024sn
          +apkv} selects, for each attention head, the prompt positions t
          +hat receive the most attention from an observation window at t
          +he end of the prompt. L2Norm \citep{devoto2024l2norm} keeps th
          +e tokens whose keys have the lowest $L_2$ norm, which correlat
          +es with high attention, without computing attention scores. Ke
          +yDiff \citep{park2025keydiff} also avoids attention scores, ke
          +eping keys that are geometrically distinctive from the others,
          + which makes it compatible with FlashAttention \citep{dao2024f
          +lashattention2}. QUOKA \citep{jones2026quoka} selects key-valu
          +e pairs for prefill from the keys aligned with a subset of rep
          +resentative queries. These methods decide which tokens to keep
          +; how much cache each layer should receive is a separate quest
          +ion, which MOSAIC addresses.                                  
      134  
      135  \textbf{Static and dynamic budget allocation.} A second line o
           f work allocates a fixed total budget non-uniformly instead of
            changing how tokens are scored. Dynamic methods recompute the
            allocation for every prompt, as dynamic quantization computes
            its ranges at run time: Ada-KV \citep{feng2025adakv} allocate
           s budget adaptively across the heads of a layer, CAKE \citep{q
           in2025cake} derives per-layer budgets from layer preferences m
           easured on each prompt's attention patterns, and SqueezeAttent
           ion \citep{wang2025squeezeattention} shifts budget between two
            layer groups. Static methods fix the allocation before infere
           nce: PyramidKV \citep{cai2025pyramidkv} assigns layer budgets 
           following a hand-designed pyramidal shape, larger in lower lay
           ers and smaller in higher ones, as does PyramidInfer \citep{ya
           ng2024pyramidinfer}; HeadKV \citep{fu2025headkv} and DuoAttent
           ion \citep{xiao2025duoattention} fix head-level allocations of
           fline. MOSAIC is static in the sense of static quantization, c
           alibrating the allocation offline for each model and eviction 
           method. Closest to our work, EvolKV \citep{yu2025evolkv} treat
           s per-layer budgets as optimization variables, partitions laye
           rs into groups, and runs evolutionary search on one group at a
            time against downstream task score at one target budget; its 
           main results then extend that allocation to larger budgets by 
           proportional rescaling, without further optimization. MOSAIC s
           hares this rescaling step but finds the allocation to rescale 
           differently, searching all layers jointly across budgets rathe
           r than at one target budget (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv}).

  Location: Introduction
  References added: PagedAttention (SOSP 2023) on KV-cache memory growth; GPTQ

  CMA-ES (Hansen & Ostermeier 2001) where EvolKV is introduced
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Location: Related Work: eviction
  References added: StreamingLLM (ICLR 2024), Scissorhands (NeurIPS 2023),
  FastGen (ICLR 2024); FlashAttention-2 (ICLR 2024)
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Location: Related Work: allocation
  References added: SqueezeAttention (ICLR 2025), PyramidInfer (Findings ACL
  2024), HeadKV (ICLR 2025), DuoAttention (ICLR 2025)
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Location: Method
  References added: Latin hypercube sampling (McKay et al. 1979), non-dominated
  sorting (NSGA-II, 2002), differential evolution (Storn & Price 1997), and
  BORE (ICML 2021) as the closest classifier-based Bayesian optimization method
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Location: Setup

  RULER (COLM 2024)
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Location: New appendix section, "Further Related Work" (linked from Related
  Work)
  References added: Quest (ICML 2024), KIVI (ICML 2024), KVQuant (NeurIPS 2024),

  MiniCache (NeurIPS 2024), Once-for-All (ICLR 2020), DARTS (ICLR 2019)

      127  \textbf{MOSAIC versus EvolKV.}\label{sec:intro-evolkv} The clo
           sest prior work, EvolKV \citep{yu2025evolkv}, searches per-lay
           er budgets with CMA-ES \citep{hansen2001cmaes} group by group,
            eight layers at a time, at a target budget fixed in advance. 
           MOSAIC instead searches all layer budgets jointly, so one sear
           ch spans about $10^{40}$ times more allocations than one EvolK
           V group search, across a budget--score Pareto front, selects a
            reusable anchor, and optionally refines it at each deployment
            budget; on Code it beats EvolKV at every budget, both searchi
           ng once ($+1.3$ to $+2.1$) and per budget at EvolKV's compute 
           ($+0.8$ to $+1.7$, Appendix~\ref{app:cost}), and even searched
            once, MOSAIC's winner outperforms EvolKV's per-budget searche
           s at every budget where both ran (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv}).

      132  
      133  \textbf{Token eviction.} Eviction methods reduce KV-cache memo
           ry by retaining only the tokens judged important. H2O \citep{z
           hang2023h2o} keeps ``heavy hitters'', tokens with high accumul
           ated attention, together with a window of recent tokens, as do
            StreamingLLM \citep{xiao2024streamingllm}, Scissorhands \cite
           p{liu2023scissorhands} and FastGen \citep{ge2024fastgen} with 
           sink, persistent and per-head criteria. SnapKV \citep{li2024sn
           apkv} selects, for each attention head, the prompt positions t
           hat receive the most attention from an observation window at t
           he end of the prompt. L2Norm \citep{devoto2024l2norm} keeps th
           e tokens whose keys have the lowest $L_2$ norm, which correlat
           es with high attention, without computing attention scores. Ke
           yDiff \citep{park2025keydiff} also avoids attention scores, ke
           eping keys that are geometrically distinctive from the others,
            which makes it compatible with FlashAttention \citep{dao2024f
           lashattention2}. QUOKA \citep{jones2026quoka} selects key-valu
           e pairs for prefill from the keys aligned with a subset of rep
           resentative queries. These methods decide which tokens to keep
           ; how much cache each layer should receive is a separate quest
           ion, which MOSAIC addresses.
      134

          -s budget adaptively across the heads of a layer, CAKE \citep{q
          -in2025cake} derives per-layer budgets from layer preferences m
          -easured on each prompt's attention patterns, and SqueezeAttent
          -ion \citep{wang2025squeezeattention} shifts budget between two

          +s budget adaptively across the heads of a layer, CAKE \citep{q
          +in2025cake} derives per-layer budgets from layer preferences m

          + layer groups. Static methods fix the allocation before infere

          +ers and smaller in higher ones; PyramidInfer \citep{yang2024py
          +ramidinfer} instead keeps, layer by layer, the context that at
          +tention weights consistently select, which shrinks with depth;
          + HeadKV \citep{fu2025headkv} and DuoAttention \citep{xiao2025d
          +uoattention} fix head-level allocations offline. MOSAIC is sta
          +tic in the sense of static quantization, calibrating the alloc
          +ation offline for each model and eviction method. Closest to o
          +ur work, EvolKV \citep{yu2025evolkv} treats per-layer budgets 
          +as optimization variables, partitions layers into groups, and 
          +runs evolutionary search on one group at a time against downst
          +ream task score at one target budget; its main results then ex
          +tend that allocation to larger budgets by proportional rescali
          +ng, without further optimization. MOSAIC shares this rescaling
          + step but finds the allocation to rescale differently, searchi
          +ng all layers jointly across budgets rather than at one target
          + budget (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv}).                           
      136  
      137  \textbf{Neural architecture search.} Multi-objective NAS trade
           s off competing goals such as accuracy and latency along a Par
           eto front \citep{elsken2018neural} (more related work in Appen
           dix~\ref{app:related}). MOSAIC adopts this multi-objective for
           mulation for KV-cache allocation but uses its own search proce
           dure (Section~\ref{sec:method}): a classifier-guided optimizer
            built for this problem, which needs only a few hundred evalua
           tions per search.

      124  
      125  This paper introduces MOSAIC, a method that automatically opti
           mizes per-layer KV-cache budgets under a target memory constra
           int using multi-objective neural architecture search. Rather t
           han hand-tuning layer-specific heuristics or optimizing layers
            group by group, MOSAIC searches the per-layer budget space jo
           intly, one budget per decoder layer (32 for Llama-3-8B, up to 
           $10^{27}$ configurations on its search grid), using Bayesian o
           ptimization guided by a surrogate MLP (Figure~\ref{fig:method}
           ). MOSAIC is to KV-cache allocation what static quantization i
           s to model quantization: just as post-training quantization ca
           librates offline on a small calibration set \citep{frantar2023
           gptq,xiao2023smoothquant}, MOSAIC fixes each layer's budget of
           fline on calibration data, so inference adds no per-prompt all
           ocation step. Methods such as CAKE and Ada-KV instead adapt th
           e budget to each prompt at inference time, as dynamic quantiza
           tion computes its ranges at run time. We evaluate MOSAIC acros
           s four eviction methods (SnapKV, H2O, AdaKV, L2Norm) on Llama-
           3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (all four methods; 
           on LongBench Summarization, SnapKV, H2O and AdaKV ran Stage 1 
           only), on two benchmarks: LongBench (4 task categories) and RU
           LER (11 in-context retrieval subtasks). On RULER, per-layer al
           location yields large gains over uniform (+2.3 to +47.9 points
           ), concentrated on the hardest needle-retrieval subtasks. On L
           ongBench, MOSAIC improves every Code setting, with dataset-lev
           el gains of up to +11.9 points on LCC (L2Norm), +3.5 on LCC fo
           r SnapKV, and +3.0 on MultiFieldQA-en (H2O) and Qasper (AdaKV)
            (Section~\ref{sec:which-stage}).

          -easured on each prompt's attention patterns, and SqueezeAttent
          -ion \citep{wang2025squeezeattention} shifts budget between two
          - layer groups. Static methods fix the allocation before infere
          -nce: PyramidKV \citep{cai2025pyramidkv} assigns layer budgets 
          -following a hand-designed pyramidal shape, larger in lower lay
          -ers and smaller in higher ones; PyramidInfer \citep{yang2024py
          -ramidinfer} instead keeps, layer by layer, the context that at
          -tention weights consistently select, which shrinks with depth;
          - HeadKV \citep{fu2025headkv} and DuoAttention \citep{xiao2025d
          -uoattention} fix head-level allocations offline. MOSAIC is sta
          -tic in the sense of static quantization, calibrating the alloc
          -ation offline for each model and eviction method. Closest to o
          -ur work, EvolKV \citep{yu2025evolkv} treats per-layer budgets 
          -as optimization variables, partitions layers into groups, and 
          -runs evolutionary search on one group at a time against downst
          -ream task score at one target budget; its main results then ex
          -tend that allocation to larger budgets by proportional rescali
          -ng, without further optimization. MOSAIC shares this rescaling
          - step but finds the allocation to rescale differently, searchi
          -ng all layers jointly across budgets rather than at one target
          - budget (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv}).                           
      135 +\textbf{Static and dynamic budget allocation.} A second line o
          +f work allocates a fixed total budget non-uniformly instead of
          + changing how tokens are scored. Dynamic methods recompute the
          + allocation for every prompt, as dynamic quantization computes
          + its ranges at run time: Ada-KV \citep{feng2025adakv} allocate
          +s budget adaptively across the heads of a layer, CAKE \citep{q
          +in2025cake} derives per-layer budgets from layer preferences m
          +easured on each prompt's attention patterns, and SqueezeAttent
          +ion \citep{wang2025squeezeattention} shifts budget between two
          + layer groups. Static methods fix the allocation before infere
          +nce: PyramidKV \citep{cai2025pyramidkv} assigns layer budgets 
          +following a hand-designed pyramidal shape, larger in lower lay
          +ers and smaller in higher ones; PyramidInfer \citep{yang2024py
          +ramidinfer} keeps per layer the context attention consistently
          + selects, less with depth; HeadKV \citep{fu2025headkv} and Duo
          +Attention \citep{xiao2025duoattention} fix head-level allocati
          +ons offline. MOSAIC is static in the sense of static quantizat
          +ion, calibrating the allocation offline for each model and evi
          +ction method. Closest to our work, EvolKV \citep{yu2025evolkv}
          + treats per-layer budgets as optimization variables, partition
          +s layers into groups, and runs evolutionary search on one grou
          +p at a time against downstream task score at one target budget
          +; its main results then extend that allocation to larger budge
          +ts by proportional rescaling, without further optimization. MO
          +SAIC shares this rescaling step but finds the allocation to re
          +scale differently, searching all layers jointly across budgets
          + rather than at one target budget (Section~\ref{sec:evolkv}). 
      136  
      137  \textbf{Neural architecture search.} Multi-objective NAS trade
           s off competing goals such as accuracy and latency along a Par
           eto front \citep{elsken2018neural} (more related work in Appen
           dix~\ref{app:related}). MOSAIC adopts this multi-objective for
           mulation for KV-cache allocation but uses its own search proce
           dure (Section~\ref{sec:method}): a classifier-guided optimizer
            built for this problem, which needs only a few hundred evalua
           tions per search.

● I applied all four Codex points, after checking each one against the source:

  - PyramidKV author list: fixed. arXiv (2406.02069) and the COLM 2025
    accepted-papers page both list 11 authors; I added the missing Yuliang Liu
    and Yucheng Li in the right positions.
  - PyramidInfer description: it no longer reads like PyramidKV. It now says
    PyramidInfer "keeps per layer the context attention consistently selects,
    less with depth", which matches its abstract (layer-wise retention of
    crucial context, chosen by consistency in attention weights).
  - Quantization analogy: the qualifying clause now reads "just as post-training
    quantization calibrates offline on a small calibration set", citing GPTQ
    and SmoothQuant. That holds for both weight and activation quantization, so
    GPTQ fits.
  - Layer-heterogeneity claim: "This overlooks a critical insight: different
    layers prioritize tokens differently" is now "These schemes already exploit
    layer differences; MOSAIC instead searches all layers jointly once and
    transfers the result to every budget." The other "same budget" sentences
    describe the eviction methods themselves, which do default to uniform layer
    budgets, so I left them.

  The build is clean: 0 errors, no undefined citations, 0 BibTeX warnings, 26
  pages. The Conclusion ends on page 8 and Limitations starts on page 9.

● This is the abstract as it currently stands in main.tex, converted to Markdown
  with the same bolding:

  ---

  The Key-Value (KV) cache is the main memory bottleneck of long-context LLM
  inference. Token eviction methods such as SnapKV, H2O, AdaKV and L2Norm shrink
  it, but they give every transformer layer the same budget, although layers
  differ in which tokens they need. We present MOSAIC, a multi-objective neural
  architecture search that learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for any eviction
  method. One search maps the trade-off between average budget and task score;
  its best allocation transfers to every target budget without further search,
  and an optional budget-constrained search refines it. Across four eviction
  methods on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, MOSAIC beats
  uniform allocation in 146 of 154 (task, method, budget) settings, by up to +48
  points on RULER and +11.9 on LongBench (LCC). It reaches the score of uniform
  allocation with up to 4× less KV cache (75% smaller), and with half the cache
  or less in 17 Llama settings. The transferred allocation alone beats uniform
  in 75 of 87 Llama settings, so a single 9–40 GPU-hour search serves every 
  budget. Against EvolKV, MOSAIC explores a ~10⁴⁰× larger search space with 4× 
  fewer evaluations and 18% fewer GPU-hours per budget, and scores higher in 5 
  of 6 settings. The learned allocations consistently favour a small set of
  middle layers.

  ---
